items.q: (A) No sooner the bell had rung than the students, (B) most of whom had been waiting impatiently, (C) poured out of the classroom (D) into the corridor.
options: No sooner the bell had rung
most of whom had been waiting impatiently
items.correction: No sooner had the bell rung
items.explanation: After a negative adverbial such as No sooner at the start of a sentence, the auxiliary and subject invert: No sooner had the bell rung than.

items.q: The committee (A) demanded that the athlete (B) returns the medal (C) immediately, (D) claiming that the test results left no room for doubt.
options: claiming that the test results left no room for doubt
items.correction: return the medal
items.explanation: Verbs such as demand, insist, suggest, recommend are followed by a that-clause in the subjunctive, so the verb takes its base form: demanded that the athlete return.

items.q: Looking at the (A) faded photographs, my grandfather (B) often says he (C) wishes he (D) would have stayed in touch with his old shipmates.
items.correction: had stayed in touch
items.explanation: A regret about the past after wish takes the past perfect (wishes he had stayed); would have belongs in a conditional result clause, not after wish.

items.q: If the volcano (A) had not erupted in 1815, crops (B) across Europe would not have failed and farmers (C) would not have to endure (D) the year without a summer.
options: across Europe would not have failed
items.correction: would not have had to endure
items.explanation: Both results of this third conditional lie in the past, so the second result also needs would have + past participle: would not have had to endure.

items.q: (A) What impressed the judges most (B) were the way the young pianist (C) handled the slow movement (D) rather than her flawless technique.
options: were the way the young pianist
items.correction: was the way the young pianist
items.explanation: In a wh-cleft sentence the what-clause is a singular subject, so the verb is singular: What impressed the judges most was the way.

items.q: (A) A large amount of tourists (B) are drawn to the island each summer, (C) putting pressure on (D) its limited supply of fresh water.
options: are drawn to the island each summer
its limited supply of fresh water
items.correction: A large number of tourists
items.explanation: Amount of goes with uncountable nouns; countable plural nouns like tourists take a large number of.

items.q: Marathon runners are advised (A) to hydrate steadily, (B) eating carbohydrates the night before, and (C) to avoid (D) anything unfamiliar on race day.
items.correction: to eat carbohydrates the night before
items.explanation: Items in a list must be parallel: the other two pieces of advice are to-infinitives (to hydrate, to avoid), so the middle one must be to eat, not an -ing form.

items.q: Rarely (A) has a single discovery (B) transformed medicine as profoundly as penicillin did, (C) nor scientists have found a substitute (D) that works so broadly.
options: transformed medicine as profoundly as penicillin did
nor scientists have found a substitute
items.correction: nor have scientists found a substitute
items.explanation: A clause introduced by nor (like neither) requires subject–auxiliary inversion: nor have scientists found.

items.q: (A) Having pored over the archives for months, the historian (B) finally came across a letter (C) that shed light on (D) why the ceasefire had broken out so abruptly.
options: Having pored over the archives for months
why the ceasefire had broken out so abruptly
items.correction: why the ceasefire had broken down so abruptly
items.explanation: Wars, fires and epidemics break out (begin suddenly); agreements, talks and ceasefires break down (collapse).

items.q: (A) Walking along the cliff path, the lighthouse (B) came into view, (C) its white tower (D) gleaming in the late afternoon sun.
options: Walking along the cliff path, the lighthouse
gleaming in the late afternoon sun
items.correction: As we walked along the cliff path, the lighthouse
items.explanation: A dangling participle: the subject of the main clause must be the one doing the walking, and a lighthouse cannot walk, so the participle clause needs its own subject.

items.q: The manuscript, (A) having been (B) written in a dialect (C) understanding by few scholars, (D) remained untranslated for over a century.
options: remained untranslated for over a century
items.correction: understood by few scholars
items.explanation: A reduced relative clause with a passive meaning (a dialect which was understood by few) uses the past participle understood, not the present participle.

items.q: If my grandmother (A) had not emigrated in 1975, I (B) would probably have been speaking Vietnamese (C) at home today (D) instead of English.
options: would probably have been speaking Vietnamese
items.correction: would probably be speaking Vietnamese
items.explanation: This is a mixed conditional: a past condition (had not emigrated) with a present result marked by today, so the result clause takes would be speaking, not the perfect form.

items.q: (A) If only I had known how steep the trail was, I (B) would have worn (C) proper boots instead of (D) the trainers I had bought them for the gym.
options: If only I had known how steep the trail was
the trainers I had bought them for the gym
items.correction: the trainers I had bought for the gym
items.explanation: In a defining relative clause with the pronoun omitted, the noun trainers is already the object of bought, so the extra object pronoun them must be dropped.

items.q: The government has (A) done several measures (B) to curb inflation, (C) none of which (D) has had a noticeable effect so far.
options: has had a noticeable effect so far
items.correction: taken several measures
items.explanation: The verb that collocates with measures in the sense of official steps is take: take measures to curb inflation.

items.q: Only after (A) the last guest had left (B) did the host (C) allow herself to admit (D) how exhausting had the evening been.
options: how exhausting had the evening been
items.correction: how exhausting the evening had been
items.explanation: The inversion triggered by Only after applies to the main clause (did the host allow); an embedded clause after admit keeps normal subject–verb order: how exhausting the evening had been.

items.q: (A) The guide, (B) not wanted to alarm the children, (C) described the approaching storm (D) as a bit of weather.
options: not wanted to alarm the children
items.correction: not wanting to alarm the children
items.explanation: A participle clause giving the reason for an action is active here (the guide did not want), so it needs the present participle not wanting, not the past participle.

items.q: Although the detectives (A) had interviewed dozens of witnesses, they (B) had uncovered (C) surprisingly few evidence (D) that would stand up in court.
options: that would stand up in court
items.correction: surprisingly little evidence
items.explanation: Evidence is uncountable, so it takes little; few is used only with plural countable nouns.

items.q: The new curriculum (A) aims to teach students (B) not only to analyse data (C) accurately but also (D) presenting their findings persuasively.
items.correction: to present their findings persuasively
items.explanation: The structures after not only … but also must be parallel: to analyse … to present, so the -ing form breaks the pattern.

items.q: (A) Little the explorers realised that the frozen river (B) on which they were travelling (C) would begin to break up (D) within a matter of hours.
items.correction: Little did the explorers realise
items.explanation: When the negative adverb Little opens a sentence, the auxiliary did is inserted before the subject and the main verb returns to its base form.

items.q: Before the students (A) were allowed to (B) handle the chemicals, the teacher (C) made a short experiment (D) to demonstrate how violently sodium reacts with water.
options: to demonstrate how violently sodium reacts with water
items.correction: carried out a short experiment
items.explanation: In English you carry out, conduct or do an experiment; make an experiment is a false collocation.

items.q: By the time the coastguard (A) finally reached them, the two fishermen (B) have spent three nights adrift (C) with nothing but (D) a single bottle of water between them.
options: a single bottle of water between them
items.correction: had spent three nights adrift
items.explanation: By the time + past simple marks a point in the past, and an action completed before that point takes the past perfect: had spent.

items.q: The twins are so alike that (A) even their teachers (B) struggle to tell (C) one from another, (D) especially when they wear identical uniforms.
options: especially when they wear identical uniforms
items.correction: one from the other
items.explanation: With exactly two people the pair is one … the other; one … another implies a group of three or more.

items.q: The residents' petition, signed by two thousand people, (A) urges that the council reconsiders its plan (B) to close the library, (C) which serves (D) a largely elderly community.
options: urges that the council reconsiders its plan
items.correction: urges that the council reconsider its plan
items.explanation: After urge that (like suggest, demand, request) the that-clause takes the subjunctive base form reconsider, with no third-person -s.

items.q: The old map (A) proved useless (B) when we reached the village, (C) most of the roads (D) having renamed since the map was drawn.
options: having renamed since the map was drawn
items.correction: having been renamed since the map was drawn
items.explanation: The roads did not rename anything; they were renamed, so the absolute participle clause needs the passive perfect form having been renamed.

items.q: The report (A) attributes the sharp decline in bee populations with pesticide use, (B) although it (C) concedes that habitat loss (D) may play an equally significant role.
options: attributes the sharp decline in bee populations with pesticide use
may play an equally significant role
items.correction: attributes the sharp decline in bee populations to pesticide use
items.explanation: The verb pattern is attribute X to Y: an effect is attributed to its cause, never with.

items.q: The old software (A) was phased out gradually (B) so that staff could get used to work with the new system (C) before the servers (D) were switched off.
options: so that staff could get used to work with the new system
items.correction: so that staff could get used to working with the new system
items.explanation: In get used to the word to is a preposition, so it is followed by a noun or -ing form: get used to working.

items.q: When the reporter (A) asked the returning astronaut (B) what she had missed most, she (C) laughed and said that (D) what did she want was a peach.
options: what did she want was a peach
items.correction: what she wanted was a peach
items.explanation: Inside reported speech a wh-clause keeps statement word order and back-shifts the tense; question inversion with did is not used: what she wanted was a peach.

items.q: (A) Far from being the easier of the three routes, the northern approach (B) turned out to be (C) by far the most treacherous, (D) as several climbers discovered.
options: Far from being the easier of the three routes
items.correction: Far from being the easiest of the three routes
items.explanation: Comparing three or more items requires the superlative: the easiest of the three; the comparative easier is only for two.

items.q: (A) With the exam only hours away, (B) I really wish (C) my brother stops practising the drums (D) in the room next to mine.
options: With the exam only hours away
my brother stops practising the drums
in the room next to mine
items.correction: my brother would stop practising the drums
items.explanation: A wish that someone else changes an annoying present habit is expressed with wish + would: I wish my brother would stop; a present-simple verb is not used after wish for this meaning.

items.q: The (A) sheer scale of the decline (B) astonished the biologists, (C) some of whom had spent decades (D) investigating the species' reluctant to breed in captivity.
options: some of whom had spent decades
investigating the species' reluctant to breed in captivity
items.correction: investigating the species' reluctance to breed in captivity
items.explanation: After a possessive (the species') the head of the phrase must be a noun, so the adjective reluctant must become the nominalised form reluctance.
